title: Dot product as similarity
story:
The dot product multiplies two vectors elementwise and adds the results. That is the whole definition, and it is worth being clear about what the number means: it is large when the two vectors point the same way and have some length to them, zero when they are at right angles, and negative when they point apart. Divide it by the two lengths and the magnitudes drop out, leaving the cosine of the angle between them — a pure measure of direction, indifferent to how long either vector is.

That indifference is why it became the standard notion of similarity. A document mentioning a word forty times and one mentioning it four times point in nearly the same direction; the cosine says they are alike, while a raw distance would say they are far apart. Salton, Wong and Yang built the vector space model on that idea in 1975, for an environment in which stored entities are compared with each other or with incoming search requests, arguing that the best indexing space is the one where each entity lies as far from the others as possible — so that the value of the system is a function of the density of the space, with retrieval performance running inversely to that density. Spread things out, and comparison becomes meaningful.

Everything called an embedding since is that idea with the coordinates learned rather than counted. When Mikolov, Chen, Corrado and Dean reported in 2013 that similarity of word representations goes beyond simple syntactic regularities, the demonstration was arithmetic: the vector for King minus the vector for Man plus the vector for Woman gives a vector close to the expected answer. Three hundred dimensions for a million-word vocabulary, from a corpus of 1.6 billion words, in under a day on one processor. It is a genuinely astonishing result and it launched a decade of work.

It is also doing less than the folklore says, and this is the part worth carrying. Linzen showed that the standard evaluation excludes the three query words from the pool of candidate answers — and that this exclusion is load-bearing. Without it, the nearest neighbour of the computed vector is the third query word itself in 93% of cases and the second in 5%. The arithmetic mostly returns one of its own inputs; the famous answer only appears because its competitors have been banned from the ballot.

The rest of that paper is the same lesson in different clothes. A baseline that ignores the offset entirely and returns the nearest neighbour of the third word reaches 0.70 accuracy on plurals. The offset method's accuracy swings from 0.13 to 0.90 depending on category. Reverse the direction of each analogy and accuracy falls by 0.11 on average, with the drop tracking the drop in that offset-ignoring baseline at a correlation of 0.72 — which, as Linzen reads it, means the method is jointly measuring whether the offsets are consistent and whether the answer was already the nearest neighbour. The geometry is real. It is just not carrying as much of the weight as the demonstration implies.

problem.name: Cosine similarity
problem.shape: Two things have to be compared for likeness, and likeness is not a quantity either of them carries.
tell: items are represented as vectors and something needs ranking by relevance
the comparison should not care how long or frequent an item is
a result is produced by taking a nearest neighbour in a learned space
vector arithmetic is being read as though it were reasoning
problem.move: Represent the items as vectors, take the dot product for alignment, and divide by the lengths when magnitude should not count. Then check what the space itself is doing: whether items are spread out enough for distances to discriminate, and whether a reported result survives the removal of whatever filtering the evaluation applied.
problem.invariant: The dot product measures alignment and the cosine measures direction alone. Any claim about meaning rests entirely on the space having been built so that direction corresponds to meaning.
problem.breaks: The measure cannot distinguish structure from crowding. In a dense region everything is close to everything, so a nearest neighbour is dominated by which points happen to lie nearby rather than by the relation you were computing — which is why an offset method's score partly reflects neighbourhood structure rather than the offset.

cost.time: one multiply-add per dimension, which is why this scales to millions of items and is the reason the whole approach is practical
cost.space: the vectors themselves, one per item, at whatever dimension the space was built with
cost.beats: exact matching, which finds only what was written the same way, and raw distance, which confuses length with dissimilarity

worked.problem: Why does the vector for King minus Man plus Woman land near the expected answer, and how much should you trust that?
worked.reasoning:
Partly the arithmetic, and more of the protocol than anyone quoting the result tends to mention.

Start with what is genuinely true. The dot product measures alignment, and normalised by the two lengths it is the cosine of the angle, which makes it a measure of direction alone. Learned embeddings place words so that co-occurrence patterns become geometry, and in such a space some relations really are carried by consistent offsets — the reported result is that the vector for King minus Man plus Woman lands close to the expected answer, and that is not nothing.

Now the protocol. The standard evaluation removes the three query words from the candidate pool before looking for a nearest neighbour. That step sounds like housekeeping and is not. Linzen measured what happens without it: the nearest neighbour of the computed vector is the third query word itself in 93% of cases, and the second in 5%. So the arithmetic, left to itself, overwhelmingly returns one of its own inputs. The famous answer wins because the three words that would otherwise beat it are disqualified.

The supporting evidence points the same way. A baseline that discards the offset altogether — ignore the first two words entirely, return the nearest neighbour of the third — gets 0.70 on the plurals category. The offset method's accuracy ranges from 0.13 to 0.90 across categories, which is not the profile of a single mechanism working uniformly. And when the analogies are reversed, accuracy drops by 0.11 on average, with the per-category drop correlating at 0.72 with the drop in that offset-ignoring baseline. Linzen's reading is that the task jointly measures offset consistency and the probability that the target was simply the nearest neighbour of the third word.

So how much to trust it: as a demonstration that these spaces have linear structure, somewhat — the offset methods did always beat the baselines. As evidence that vector arithmetic performs analogical reasoning, much less, because a large part of the score is neighbourhood structure rather than the offset. And as an evaluation metric for a new embedding space, treat a number produced this way as uninterpretable unless the baselines are reported next to it.

The transferable habit is the one this exposes: when a result depends on a filtering step, measure what the step is doing. Here the filter was discarding the answer the method actually wanted to give, 93% of the time.

problem.practice: Take an embedding space and run an analogy without excluding the query words from the candidate pool. Record how often the answer is simply one of the inputs. Then implement the baseline that ignores the offset entirely and returns the nearest neighbour of the third word, and compare the two scores category by category.

beats.broke: Meaning has to be compared and comparison needs a number, but words, documents and images arrive with no natural notion of distance between them.
beats.fix: Place them as vectors and let the dot product measure alignment — divided by the two lengths it becomes the cosine of the angle, a measure of direction alone, which is the whole machinery behind every notion of similarity in retrieval and embeddings.
beats.cost: The geometry is only as meaningful as the space it was built in, and arithmetic that reads like reasoning can be dominated by which points happen to lie near which others rather than by the relation being computed.

interview.q: Why does the vector for King minus Man plus Woman land near the expected answer, and how much should you trust that?
interview.trap: Taking it as a demonstration that the space performs analogical reasoning. Remove the rule excluding the query words and the method returns one of its own inputs 93% of the time, so a large part of the celebrated result is the evaluation protocol.
interview.answer:
Partly the arithmetic, and considerably more of the evaluation protocol than the usual telling admits.

What is genuinely true first. The dot product measures alignment, and divided by the two lengths it is the cosine of the angle, so it captures direction alone. Learned embeddings arrange words so that co-occurrence becomes geometry, and some relations really are carried by consistent offsets — the reported result is that the vector for King minus Man plus Woman lands near the expected answer, and that is a real phenomenon.

Then the protocol. The standard evaluation excludes the three query words from the candidate pool before taking a nearest neighbour, and that step turns out to be load-bearing rather than housekeeping. Without it, the nearest neighbour of the computed vector is the third query word itself in 93% of cases and the second in 5%. The arithmetic left to itself overwhelmingly returns one of its own inputs; the celebrated answer wins because the words that would have beaten it were disqualified.

The rest of the evidence agrees. A baseline that throws the offset away entirely — ignore the first two words, return the nearest neighbour of the third — scores 0.70 on plurals. The offset method's accuracy ranges from 0.13 to 0.90 across categories, which is not what a single uniform mechanism looks like. Reversing the analogies costs 0.11 on average, and the per-category drop correlates at 0.72 with the drop in that offset-ignoring baseline, which suggests the task is jointly measuring offset consistency and whether the answer was already the nearest neighbour of the third word.

So: as evidence that these spaces contain linear structure, it holds up, since the offset methods did consistently beat the baselines. As evidence that vector arithmetic is doing analogical reasoning, much weaker. And as a metric for evaluating a new space, a number reported without those baselines beside it is not interpretable.

The habit worth taking from it is general: when a result depends on a filtering step, measure what the filter is removing. Here it was removing the answer the method actually preferred, 93% of the time.

blueprint:
DOT PRODUCT -> COSINE -> "SIMILARITY"

   a . b            alignment, scaled by lengths
   a . b / |a||b|   direction ONLY

   this is the whole machinery behind every
   "similar items" you have ever seen.

THE 1975 FRAMING, STILL CORRECT

   compare stored entities with each other, or
   with an incoming request.

   best space = entities as far apart as possible
   value of the system ~ f(density)
   retrieval performance ~ INVERSE of density

EMBEDDINGS

   same geometry, coordinates LEARNED from
   co-occurrence instead of counted.

   2013: vec(King) - vec(Man) + vec(Woman)

THE CORRECTION, IN ONE NUMBER

   remove the exclusion rule and the nearest
   neighbour of a* - a + b is:

      b   (an INPUT)        93%
      a*  (an INPUT)         5%
      a                    never

   the method's preferred answer is its own input.
   "queen" wins a race its rivals were barred from.

SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

   ignore the offset, return nearest neighbour
   of the third word:     0.70 on plurals
   offset method range:   0.13 - 0.90
   reverse direction:     -0.11 average
                          r = 0.72 with the
                          baseline's own drop

THE HABIT THIS TEACHES

   when a result depends on a FILTERING step,
   measure what the step is doing.

   here the filter was discarding the answer the
   method actually wanted to give, 93% of the
   time.
takeaway: The dot product normalised by the lengths is the cosine, and that single number is what every embedding means by similar — but a result computed in such a space can be carried by crowding rather than by structure, which is why the famous analogy returns one of its own inputs once the filter is removed.
